item.title: On the Tragedy of the Commons in Heterogeneous Distributed Resource Allocation
item.description: arXiv:2611.33172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the Tragedy of the Commons (ToC) problem, which commonly arises in heterogeneous distributed resource allocation, in which selfish users are independently interested in optimizing their own utility. Such self-interested decision-making in decentralized settings often results in inefficient resource utilization because users prefer high-capacity resources, leading to their overutilization. We cast the problem into a non-cooperative game and derive closed-form characterizations of both the distributed Nash equilibrium (NE) and the socially optimal allocation. In view of these closed-form expressions, we establish the structural conditions under which the ToC arises, and derive an exact expression for the Price of Anarchy (PoA). We further prove that the PoA can become arbitrarily large (unbounded) under suitable traffic conditions. Motivated by these observations, we propose a penalty-based incentive mechanism that discourages the use of overloaded servers while preserving decentralized decision-making. We analyze the resulting equilibrium load redistribution and establish conditions under which the proposed mechanism reduces the overall system cost and improves equilibrium efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Avadh Kishor, Rajdeep Niyogi

item.title: Soft Decentralized Expected SARSA: Equilibrium Selection via Gradual Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2611.33228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Soft Decentralized Expected SARSA (SDES), a modification of Decentralized Q-learning in which agents maintain persistent exploration and update their acting Q-values gradually rather than switching directly to newly learned best responses when updating. We prove convergence to $\epsilon$-greedy Nash equilibria in weakly acyclic stochastic games for sufficiently large batch sizes. We then show, in the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with memory, that soft updating can reshape basins of attraction without changing the equilibrium set. In the deterministic limit, we derive analytical basin bounds governed by the Q-value differences between actions in the target policies and show that reducing the policy learning rate can favor either cooperative or competitive equilibria. These results suggest that soft updating is not merely a stabilization device but also a mechanism of equilibrium selection in decentralized learning.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Martucci, Janusz M. Meylahn, Gurdal Arslan, Serdar Yuksel

item.title: CypherMAS: Benchmarking Routing Reliability in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.33242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) distribute reasoning across specialized agents that must exchange messages and invoke tools reliably. Existing evaluations typically couple communication with open domain tasks, making it difficult to determine whether a failure arises from reasoning, malformed tool use, lost messages, or forgotten requests. Prior benchmarks do not isolate communication execution or measure routing redundancy against a known optimal path. We introduce CypherMAS, a synthetic benchmark that isolates communication and routing in fixed multi-agent graphs. Agents in chain, star, bipartite, or ring graphs route cyphered messages to remote peers holding the matching decoders; since the optimal route is known, redundant LLM calls can be measured and routing failures may be easily tracked. Across eleven open-weight models from 4B to 753B, small models fail at routing and tool use, dense models above 27B degrade with diameter, and successful runs exceed minimum LLM calls. These findings identify communication reliability as a distinct scaling bottleneck for multi-agent systems and provide a controlled diagnostic for complex multi-agent systems. The source code is freely available: https://github.com/Andoree/CypherMAS.
item.dc:creator: Danil Kostromin, Andrey Sakhovskiy, Semen Budennyy

item.title: What Must LLM Agents Communicate? From Information Loss to Communication Failures
item.description: arXiv:2611.33318v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When evidence is distributed across LLM agents, a team may collectively possess all the information needed for a decision yet fail to use it effectively. What must agents communicate for accurate joint predictions, and when does interaction help? We study three requirements for effective communication: sufficiency of the information conveyed, selection of relevant evidence, and utilization of received information. Drawing on information theory and communication complexity, we develop a framework that combines theoretical benchmarks with controlled experiments and message-level analyses. We find that local probability reports can discard essential information, with theoretical information loss closely matching observed performance penalties. Query-first interaction improves predictions when relevant evidence depends on a private query, but compact one-shot representations can eliminate this advantage. Even when sufficient information is communicated, agents may fail to select or use it correctly. Together, these findings distinguish fundamental communication limits from failures in how LLM agents communicate and use information.
item.dc:creator: Yi-Yun Chu, Xiaobin Shen

item.title: Welfare-Enhancing Mechanism Design for Agent Ecosystems
item.description: arXiv:2611.33627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The emerging Agentic Web forms a multi-agent ecosystem: a decentralized service market where the user agent selects which content agents to query from their submitted profiles, before seeing any documents. Profiles therefore become a new target of optimization. Existing Generative Engine Optimization studies how a single supplier rewrites documents the engine can already retrieve, to improve their citation. In the Agentic Web, multiple content agents optimize profiles to compete for limited opportunities to deliver documents. To study this repeated interaction, we build WildRegistry, a simulation framework and benchmark based on a real agentic-search request stream, and model it as a dynamic game under private monitoring. Long-horizon experiments show that this competition lowers website-selection quality and settles at a harmful stable point, which our empirical criterion identifies as an approximate rewriting equilibrium. We therefore design a welfare-enhancing mechanism, DEC (Delivery-Evidence Credit), a platform-side policy that uses recorded delivery outcomes to reallocate later opportunities and reduce information asymmetry. DEC improves this endpoint, raising website-selection quality while preserving most of providers' exposure gains, for a Welfare Gain of +2.01 points and a healthier long-horizon outcome. More broadly, our findings highlight the importance of mechanism design in agent ecosystems: turning recorded delivery outcomes into evidence that endogenously shapes later user-agent selection and content-agent adaptation can steer long-horizon adaptation toward delivered capabilities.
item.dc:creator: Zitian Guo, Chen Xu, Beibei Li, Chenyan Xiong

item.title: When Are Parallel Subagents Effective for Coding? An Empirical Study on Repository Construction
item.description: arXiv:2611.33893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based coding agents are increasingly used for long-horizon tasks such as building an entire program from a specification. Products like Codex and Claude Code let an agent delegate work to parallel subagents, multiplying run cost, yet it remains unclear whether and when delegation produces a better program. We compare a single agent with a main agent delegating to subagents on repository-construction tasks from NL2Repo and ProgramBench (which also provides an executable reference program). We compare scores at equal time and equal cost, run intervention experiments, and analyze fine-grained behavior. On randomly drawn tasks, parallel subagents raise hidden-test pass rates by only about 1 to 5 percentage points at up to 3.8x the cost of a single agent. Their gain is larger on hard tasks, where we find evidence of three mechanisms. Self-checking: with GPT-5.6 Sol, one sentence telling a single agent to probe the reference program first recovers most of this gain at a fraction of the cost; from GPT-5.6 Sol to GPT-6.1 Sol, the gain shrinks as single agents check their own work more. Fresh context: in extended runs, a single agent that periodically starts a new session with an empty conversation makes faster early progress in every comparison than one that resumes its conversation. Modularity: multi-agent runs produce more modular code (more files and shorter functions), closer to the upstream source. We observe similar patterns in a smaller replication with Opus 5.5 on Claude Code. Overall, subagents help when (i) a single agent stops checking too early, (ii) a long session keeps editing with little improvement, or (iii) modular code helps on the task; otherwise, they mainly add cost.
item.dc:creator: Zhiheng Lyu, Chengyu Yin, Lingming Zhang

item.title: Post-Training Policy Replication for Strategy-Following Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning across Team Sizes
item.description: arXiv:2611.34035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although multi-agent deep reinforcement learning enables coordinated behavior, aligning it with managerial intent remains difficult due to complex agent interactions. Although the strategy-following distributed attentional actor architecture (sfDA7-X) improves controllability via regional instructions, instruction combinations scale exponentially with team and instruction sizes, leading to prohibitive training costs and poor transferability. To reduce this computational cost, we introduce a team-size-independent observation architecture and reconstruct collective behavior by replicating a single trained policy across agents in teams of different sizes, thereby eliminating the need to train from scratch. Additionally, we evaluate warm-start retraining by initializing policy networks with a pre-trained policy to significantly lower computational overhead. In an object collection game, a policy trained in a four-agent team is deployed to teams of three to eight agents. Experiments demonstrate that training with the proposed aggregated observation matrix achieves performance comparable to that of the baseline method, sfDA7-X. Furthermore, policy replication preserves performance without substantial degradation in three- and five-agent teams, and warm-start retraining outperforms training from scratch while reducing required training episodes by up to 90%. Deployments to six- and eight-agent teams further confirm effective spatial region allocation following given instructions. These results demonstrate that the proposed method enables zero-shot collective behavior reconstruction via policy replication.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: ICAART 2027 - 19th International Conference on Agents and Artificial Intelligence, INSTICC, Feb 2027, Valletta, Malta
item.dc:creator: Yamato Takahagi, Yoshinari Motokawa, Toshiharu Sugawara

item.title: Deep Learning-Based Mesoscopic Emission Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2611.33179v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Traffic-related emissions are a major contributor to urban air pollution. However, existing emission models face a fundamental trade-off: macroscopic models are computationally efficient but rely on average speeds, leading to systematic errors, while microscopic models achieve high accuracy but are computationally prohibitive for large scale simulations. To bridge this gap, this study introduces Direct Emission Prediction (DEP), a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-based deep learning model. DEP was trained on over one million synthetic trips generated by coupling real-world GNSS speed profiles with the microscopic emission model MOBSim. By processing sequential link-level inputs, including vehicle characteristics, road attributes, and ambient temperature, DEP predicts CO$_2$ and NOx emissions. We integrated DEP into a MATSim-based workflow and applied it to the Ile-de-France region. DEP matches the accuracy of SPG-M, a hybrid mesoscopic-microscopic reference model, within 0.35% for CO$_2$ and 1.87% for NOx across both hot and cold-start scenarios, while reducing computational runtime to just 2.2%. Furthermore, validation against empirical remote sensing data confirms that DEP accurately reproduces real-world NOx emission levels across Euro 2-6 diesel vehicles, whereas traditional macroscopic tools like COPERT and HBEFA systematically underestimate them. Finally, DEP effectively captures the spatial distribution of cold-start emissions, identifying key hotspots in dense urban areas. This work demonstrates that deep learning-based mesoscopic frameworks can achieve microscopic accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost, enabling scalable, high-resolution urban emission modeling without relying on pre-computed emission factor databases.
item.dc:creator: Abdelkader Dib, Milos Balac, Antonio Sciarretta

item.title: Formalization, Transparency, and Collusion in Open-Source Game Theory
item.description: arXiv:2611.33193v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cooperation among AI agents will undermine alignment protocols when it takes the form of collusion. Under these protocols, agents often have some information about one another, and how much they have may determine whether they collude. Open-source game theory studies the extreme case, in which each program reads its opponent's source code and acts based on what it can prove about it. We develop formal foundations for this theory: we specify a concrete proof system, resolve an open problem concerning DupocBot and CupodBot through a transposition argument, and mechanize the framework in Lean 4; to our knowledge, this is the first mechanization of resource-bounded open-source game theory. We then extend the framework to the more realistic setting of partial transparency, where each program receives only partial information about its opponent. In Prisoner's Dilemma experiments, where mutual cooperation models collusion, greater transparency increases both the cooperation sustainable in equilibrium and the cooperation selected by replicator dynamics. This suggests that controlling how much agents can know about one another matters for alignment protocols.
item.dc:creator: Colomban Duclaux, Riccardo Formenti, Pepijn Cobben, Terry Jingchen Zhang, Bernhard Sch\"olkopf, Zhijing Jin

item.title: From Conversations to Commitments: A Design Study of Shared Records for Agent-to-Business Coordination
item.description: arXiv:2611.33373v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Business commitments require accepted terms to be linked to delegated authority, reserved resources and durable evidence. We examine how a shared, attributable interaction record can support these links across independently operated organisations. Talea combines signed AT Protocol records with A2A task execution. We use its coordination sandbox and a proposed commercial extension in a design study of an airline booking disrupted passengers into three competing hotels. Four observations follow. First, AT Protocol provides mechanisms supporting five of six coordination requirements, while record-level access and release controls require additional enforcement. Second, the case's confidentiality constraints restrict each hotel's authorised view to its bilateral exchange; only the airline can correlate all three deals. Third, this leaves a possible benefit for late-joining participants inside the airline's trust boundary, but does not establish an advantage over an equally instrumented point-to-point design. Fourth, a deterministic release interface constrains fixed, approved payloads but cannot bound disclosure when negotiated values depend on private state. Finite-model explorations and deterministic interface checks reproduce the specified behaviours and counterexamples when selected controls are removed. They do not measure comparative benefit or validate a deployed commercial system. The remaining hypothesis is that, within one trust boundary, shared records improve decision reconstruction and recovery under changing participation relative to point-to-point exchange with equivalent authority, reservation, retention and correlation evidence. We specify an experiment to test it.
item.dc:creator: Carlos Eberhardt (IBM Software, Rochester, United States of America), Mansura Habiba (IBM Software, Dublin, Ireland)

item.title: LSRP*-LA: Scalable and Anytime Multi-Agent Path Finding for Large Agents with Asynchronous Actions
item.description: arXiv:2611.33793v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) seeks collision-free paths for multiple agents from their start locations to their goal locations while minimizing path costs. Most MAPF algorithms assume that each agent occupies a single vertex and that the actions of all agents are synchronized. These assumptions may limit the use of MAPF planners in practice. Existing planners that get rid of both assumptions either handle only a few agents or cannot improve their solutions. Recently, a planner called LSRP* was proposed, which is scalable and anytime with asynchronous actions, but still limited by that each agent occupies a single vertex. This paper develops a new planner called LSRP*-LA for MAPF for large agents with asynchronous actions (LA-MAPF-AA), where an agent can occupy several cells. LSRP*-LA is scalable and complete, and it keeps improving solution quality after the initial solution is obtained until the runtime budget depletes. We analyze the properties of LSRP*-LA and test it against several baselines with up to 800 agents on various maps. LSRP*-LA can handle twice as many agents as baseline methods and its solution cost is about half that of recent synchronous planners for large agents.
item.dc:creator: Dachuan Liu, Shizhe Zhao, Zhongqiang Ren

item.title: Not Every Input Needs Everything: Unifying Expert Gating, Model Cascades, and Agent Orchestration
item.description: arXiv:2611.34112v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Executing monolithic neural weights, frontier foundation models, or entire multi-agent workflows uniformly on every input incurs substantial computational, latency, and monetary overhead. Conditional computation mitigates this cost by deciding dynamically which internal experts, model endpoints, or specialized agents to invoke per request. Yet token-level gating in sparse neural architectures, query-level model cascades, and task-level multi-agent coordination have largely progressed in disconnected research silos, obscuring recurring system failures and transferable fixes. In this systematic review, we synthesize 2,289 studies published between 2017 and September 2026 (selected from 13,884 unique records) across 20 methodological families under a unified two-step inspect-then-allocate framework. Discrete hard selection accounts for 70%, 83%, and 91% of token-, query-, and task-scale literature respectively, and computational overhead appears as a top operational bottleneck across every layer. Engineering safeguards remain sharply asymmetric: intra-layer gating prioritizes load balancing while rarely incorporating uncertainty estimation, whereas model selection and agent orchestration rely on confidence thresholds and budget rules while confronting miscalibration and cascading errors. At the same time, publication volume is accelerating fastest in agentic task delegation, where routing mechanisms are least often isolated experimentally and methodological bias risk is highest.
item.dc:creator: Dat Tat Mai, Hung Tran Quy, Thai Viet Pham, James Jin Kang

item.title: GRASP: Graph Agentic Search over Propositions for Multi-hop Question Answering
item.description: arXiv:2605.16598v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic retrieval improves multi-hop question answering by giving language models autonomy to iteratively gather evidence. Recent work augments these systems with knowledge graphs for structured traversal, but this combination introduces significant cost: expensive graph construction at index time and compounding token usage at inference time. We introduce Graph Agentic Search over Propositions (GRASP), an agentic system that simultaneously optimizes for high accuracy and minimal token usage in multi-hop question answering. Rather than executing a rigid, singular query, GRASP actively coordinates its retrieval strategy by decomposing multi-hop queries into dependency-aware plans. This enables GRASP to dynamically scale the number of sub-agents according to the complexity of the problem. Each sub-agent resolves its single-hop query by exploring a novel three-layer hierarchical graph of entities, propositions, and passages, using the entity layer for targeted traversal and the proposition layer for high-recall passage retrieval via reciprocal-rank voting. We evaluate GRASP on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultihopQA, and HotpotQA under two settings: open-corpus retrieval and extended context reasoning (LongBench). GRASP achieves the highest QA accuracy in the open retrieval setting on MuSiQue and 2Wiki while using 40-50 percent fewer tokens than IRCoT+HippoRAG2. Furthermore, GRASP leads on EM and F1 across all three datasets in the LongBench setting while using 30 percent fewer tokens than the next most accurate method. Finally, we introduce success economy - the amortized token cost per correct answer, weighted by difficulty - and advocate for efficiency-aware evaluation as a standard practice for agentic QA.
item.dc:creator: Stockton Jenkins, Ramya Korlakai Vinayak, Junjie Hu

item.title: PLAICraft: Large-Scale Time-Aligned Vision-Speech-Action Dataset for Embodied AI
item.description: arXiv:2505.12707v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Advances in deep generative modeling have made it increasingly plausible to train human-level embodied agents. Yet progress has been limited by the absence of large-scale, real-time, multi-modal, and socially interactive datasets that reflect the sensory-motor complexity of natural environments. To address this, we present PLAICraft, a novel data collection platform and dataset capturing multiplayer Minecraft interactions across five time-aligned modalities: video, game output audio, microphone input audio, mouse, and keyboard actions. Each modality is logged with millisecond time precision, enabling the study of synchronous, embodied behaviour in a rich, open-ended world. The dataset comprises 5525 hours of interactive gameplay from more than 232 participants. Alongside the dataset, we provide an evaluation suite for benchmarking model capabilities in object recognition, spatial awareness, language grounding, and long-term memory. PLAICraft opens a path toward training and evaluating agents that act fluently and purposefully in real time, paving the way for truly embodied artificial intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Yingchen He, Christian D. Weilbach, Martyna E. Wojciechowska, Yiyuan Sun, Jason Yoo, Yuxuan Zhang, Oluwanifemi A. Adekanye, Chia-Hong Hsu, Vasileios Lioutas, Frank Wood

item.title: Curated Collaborative AI Edge with Network Data Analytics for B5G/6G Radio Access Networks
item.description: arXiv:2507.01994v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite advancements, Radio Access Networks (RAN) still account for over 50\% of the total power consumption in 5G networks. Existing RAN split options do not fully harness data potential, presenting an opportunity to reduce operational expenditures. This paper addresses this opportunity through a twofold approach. First, highly accurate network traffic and user predictions are achieved using the proposed Curated Collaborative Learning (CCL) framework, which selectively collaborates with relevant correlated data for traffic forecasting. CCL optimally determines whom, when, and what to collaborate with, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art approaches, including global, federated, personalized federated, and cyclic institutional incremental learnings by 43.9%, 39.1%, 40.8%, and 31.35%, respectively. Second, the Distributed Unit Pooling Scheme (DUPS) is proposed, leveraging deep reinforcement learning and prediction inferences from CCL to reduce the number of active DU servers efficiently. DUPS dynamically redirects traffic from underutilized DU servers to optimize resource use, improving energy efficiency by up to 89% over conventional strategies, translating into substantial monetary benefits for operators. By integrating CCL-driven predictions with DUPS, this paper demonstrates a transformative approach for minimizing energy consumption and operational costs in 5G RANs, significantly enhancing efficiency and cost-effectiveness.
item.dc:creator: Sardar Jaffar Ali, Syed M. Raza, Duc-Tai Le, Min Young Chung, Ness Shroff, Hyunseung Choo

item.title: Equal Opportunity: A Correctness Condition for Ordered Consensus
item.description: arXiv:2509.09868v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In proof-of-stake blockchains based on State Machine Replication (SMR), the order of transactions directly affects client-visible financial outcomes. Ordered consensus augments the SMR specification by imposing correctness conditions on transaction ordering, with a focus on limiting Byzantine influence. However, real-world ordering attacks can occur even when these conditions hold, often enabled by advantages such as faster networks or proximity to the blockchain infrastructure that allow an adversary to systematically bias outcomes without violating the conditions. To address this gap, we extend ordered consensus with a new model and correctness condition based on equal opportunity, a notion of fairness widely used in legal contexts. Equal opportunity requires that candidates who are equally qualified---according to criteria deemed relevant---have equal chances of being selected (here, for a given position in the total order). We show how carefully introduced randomness can bound ordering bias, and we introduce the Secret Random Oracle (SRO), a fault-tolerant abstraction for generating such randomness. We present two SRO constructions, based on trusted hardware and threshold verifiable random functions, respectively, and use them to build Pomp\=e-SRO, a new ordered consensus protocol that mitigates well-known ordering attacks. Our evaluation shows that Pomp\=e-SRO effectively mitigates front-running and sandwich attacks at a moderate cost to latency.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 20th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 26), 2026
item.dc:creator: Yunhao Zhang, Haobin Ni, Soumya Basu, Shir Cohen, Maofan Yin, Lorenzo Alvisi, Robbert van Renesse, Qi Chen, Lidong Zhou

item.title: Mechanism-Based Intelligence: Differentiable Incentives for Rational Coordination and Equilibrium Alignment in Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2512.20688v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Autonomous multi-agent systems struggle with the Hayekian Information problem (using dispersed private knowledge) and the Hurwiczian Incentive problem (aligning local actions with global objectives). I introduce Mechanism-Based Intelligence (MBI), an architecture that treats intelligence as emergent from the coordination of specialized modules rather than a single monolithic model. At its core, the Differentiable Price Mechanism computes the exact gradient of the system loss as a price; subtracting its own marginal cost, each agent obtains the incentive signal $$\mathbf{G}_i = - \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_i},$$ and the transfers take the Groves form. Each agent's best response minimizes the global loss given the actions of others, so the negative global loss is an exact potential for the resulting game, with a unique equilibrium at the global optimum. Gradient-based play converges to it under a step-size condition when effort is costless, and stops near it otherwise: a satisficing rule halts each agent's search when its marginal gain no longer exceeds its marginal computational cost. The equilibrium requires no knowledge of agents' private costs, so asymmetric information causes no welfare loss; simultaneous gradient dynamics require only a public bound on cost curvature. Each iteration scales linearly ($\mathcal{O}(N)$) with the number of agents, though for losses summed over agents the iteration count also grows with $N$. For known, differentiable losses, MBI avoids the combinatorial search of Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes. Under convexity and smoothness conditions, MBI aligns agent self-interest with the Planner's objective, offering an auditable approach to multi-agent coordination.
item.dc:creator: Stefano Grassi

item.title: From Per-Frame Search to Practical Attacks: Investigating Adversarial Robustness of Multi-Agent Heterogeneous Cooperative Perception
item.description: arXiv:2609.17856v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Heterogeneous cooperative perception (CP) lets connected agents with different sensors and encoders share bird's-eye-view (BEV) features and align them through learned translation modules before fusion and detection. A malicious collaborator can perturb its broadcast to erase real objects from a neighbor's view, yet prior CP attacks assume homogeneous agents and rely on per-frame gradient descent that needs test-time labels, online detector queries, and slow backward passes. Porting these homogeneous attacks to heterogeneous CP exposes two further architectural barriers. Translation modules often block direct gradients, and heterogeneous fusion stacks use per-location fusion and detection heads that leave the standard removal-loss gradient zero on over $99\%$ of the attacker's message, so per-frame updates reach only the sparse anchor footprint while neighboring cells still detect the object. We present HetPoison, a practical feature attack that trains a convolutional generator once, offline, on a frozen surrogate stack to map channel-observable features to a bounded perturbation in one forward pass, requiring no labels, detector queries, or gradients online. Because the generator parameterizes perturbations across the spatial neighborhood rather than per coordinate, HetPoison overcomes sparse anchor gradients while amortizing search across frames into a $\sim$2 ms forward pass. On OPV2V-H, HetPoison lowers STAMP detection average precision from $0.899$ to $0.063$, outperforms 500-step Adam-PGD on HEAL, STAMP, and CodeFilling at up to $14{,}000\times$ lower online cost, and remains effective on real-world V2X-Real fleets and under cross-family transfer, communication delay, quantization, and unseen collaborator encoders.
item.dc:creator: Chenyi Wang, Yutong Liu, Qingzhao Zhang, Ming F. Li

item.title: Agent Calibration under Deployment Change: Acceptance Contracts, Trajectory Repair, and Adaptation Costs
item.description: arXiv:2609.35149v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: An agent can remain operational after a model, tool, or user-context change while losing capabilities required at its destination. We define agent calibration as qualification against a versioned deployment contract. The contract specifies basic capabilities and end-to-end reachability, technical and professional precision, and acceptance by intended users. For each requirement, a source-to-destination map records what must be preserved, transformed, added, or retired. Experts supply benchmarks, positive and negative examples, annotated trajectories, and cost limits. These instruments guide changes to prompts and context, tool calls and other harness settings, or an external compact policy while the foundation model remains frozen. Candidate revisions are evaluated against fixed acceptance criteria using independent evidence. We compare the costs of maintaining a harness with and without an external policy, including annotation, training, serving, review, and rework. Three diagnostic audits illustrate the limits of aggregate scores. On a 100-item intent task, each model solved cases the other missed. In a 60-record synthetic financial reporting fixture, five records passed a numeric proxy but failed the reporting contract. In a target-only WebMall snapshot, quota interruptions affected 132 of 171 attempts. These observations motivate paired reruns, checkpoint replay, and separate measurement of repaired and newly failed cases. We specify controlled experiments to test whether calibration increases accepted deliveries at a given cost.
item.dc:creator: Yaxiao Liu (PwC China AI Center), Pengbo Liu (PwC China AI Center), Yiwen Liu (PwC China AI Center), Yihua Guan (PwC China AI Center), Xingjian Li (PwC China AI Center), Jiaxing Song (Tsinghua University)

item.title: VirusCascade: Hijacking Collaborative Reflection in LLM-Powered Recommender Agents
item.description: arXiv:2609.38270v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Advancing beyond traditional static scoring models, LLM-powered agentic recommender systems (LLM-ARS) instantiate users and items as autonomous agents, whose semantic states are dynamically refined through a recurrent process known as collaborative reflection. While this mechanism improves recommendation quality, it simultaneously introduces a systemic vulnerability: adversarial evidence injected into a single agent can be rationalised into a legitimate preference narrative, written back into memory, and propagated to other agents through interaction contexts. We term the local rationalisation process reflection laundering, and its system-wide escalation through collaborative reflection collaborative-reflection hijacking. Existing attacks on recommender systems, whether based on interaction-level data poisoning or text-level adversarial perturbations, assume static pipelines and thus cannot exploit this recurrent, multi-agent amplification pathway. To bridge this gap, we first conduct a controlled vulnerability analysis that establishes two exploitable properties underlying collaborative-reflection hijacking: reflective persistence and cross-agent propagation. Then building on these findings, we propose VirusCascade, the first black-box targeted promotion attack that jointly shapes semantic and structural attack surfaces: the former ensures the target item is naturally rationalised as satisfying broad user preferences, the latter positions it for system-wide propagation. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets across diverse LLM-ARS architectures demonstrate that VirusCascade consistently achieves state-of-the-art targeted exposure under evaluated stealth constraints, reaching a mean E@20 of 0.384 and surpassing the strongest baseline by an absolute margin of +0.185.
item.dc:creator: Yurong Hao, Wen Zhou, Guowei Guan, Tiantong Wu, Fuyao Zhang, Wei Yang Bryan Lim

item.title: AgentDRC: Multi-Agent Algorithms for Spatially-Aware Automated DRC Correction
item.description: arXiv:2611.31876v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Design Rule Checking (DRC) error fixing remains a time-consuming bottleneck in physical design, often requiring manual intervention despite advanced EDA optimizations. Existing LLM-agent approaches fall short due to redundant contextual shapes, limited spatial reasoning over raw coordinates, and inefficient flat layout representations. We propose AgentDRC, which formulates iterative DRC correction as a multi-agent algorithm and introduces a spatial-aware verification and correction algorithm that reconstructs structured spatial relations among critical shapes and validates fixes through geometric and semantic constraint checking. The system coordinates four specialized agents to perceive multi-level, multi-modal geometric features, filter irrelevant shapes, and iteratively correct violations. Experiments show that AgentDRC achieves up to 30.4% pass@1 and 55.7% pass@5 on challenging violations, with 13.8% pass@5 improvement over the best baseline. We will open-source all code and benchmark tasks upon acceptance.
item.dc:creator: Pengju Liu (Katie), Nuo Xu (Katie), Winson Chen (Katie), Peijun Li (Katie), Yang (Katie), Zhao, Yu Cao, Caiwen Ding
